sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages (rev. ed.), sec. 4.3 (Borneo). Asia-Pacific Linguistics Open Access Monographs 8. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: General Borneo statement only, not Kayan-specific: 'Unlike the Philippines, stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo. However, unlike much of the AN world, where stress falls predictably on the penult, many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context.'

sources.citation: Blust, Robert A. 1977. Sketches of the morphology and phonology of Bornean languages 1: Uma Juman (Kayan). In Papers in Borneo and Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 2, 9-122. Pacific Linguistics A-33. Canberra: ANU. https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/254321
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: SISTER LANGUAGE ONLY (Uma Juman = Rejang Kayan [ree] reja1241, Balui basin, Sarawak; not xkn). Rule 8 'stress placement', printed p. 76 (PDF p. 69 of the chapter file): 'In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase.' Also p. 33 (general): stress final in citation forms but penultimate in context 'in most of the languages described'; p. 24: affixes not normally stressed, full words bear stress; p. 85: locative clitic /ha?/ never stressed in rapid speech.

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2018. Kayanic comparative vocabularies (ADS2-001). Kaipuleohone, University of Hawai'i Digital Ethnographic Archive. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/81770
sources.note: Wordlist only: 791 'Apo Kayan Kayan' (Data Dian, code xkn) forms in IPA-style transcription with vowel length (ː) marked on 123 items but no stress marks; the readme says nothing about stress.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2002. Formalism or phoneyism? The history of Kayan final glottal stop. In Adelaar & Blust (eds), Between worlds: linguistic papers in memory of David John Prentice, 29-37. Pacific Linguistics 529. https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/254131
sources.note: No mention of stress or accent (grep of full text layer). Comparative note on final glottal stop in Baram Kayan, Uma Juman, Uma Bawang, Murik; the Apau Kayan area is named once (p. 30) but no xkn data.

sources.citation: Guerreiro, Antonio J. 1996. Homophony, sound changes and dialectal variations in some central Bornean languages. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 205-226.
sources.note: Nothing on stress in any Kayan variety. It names the xkn groups (Uma' Lekan, Uma' Laran, Uma' Lasan; Apo Kayan) in lexical comparisons and lists Kayanic phonological traits (diphthongization, vowel clusters, 'lengthening of vowels in open syllables', gemination, p. ~210); the only 'unstressed' remark (p. 212) is Haudricourt's general claim about vowel dropping applied to Modang.
